strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a clearly articulated failure mode ('information self-locking') in outcome-based RL for multi-turn active reasoning, and the AS/BT decomposition is an intuitive and useful lens. The controlled experiments in Sec. 2.3 (fixing action sequences and swapping belief-update mechanisms; the 'Unknown' feedback intervention in Fig. 5a) provide genuinely careful causal evidence that disentangles the two capabilities, going beyond mere correlation.

The theoretical framework is a real strength: the policy-gradient decomposition into AS and BT channels (Eq. 1), the one-sided drift bounds (Thm. 3.4/B.14), and the finite escape-time bound (Prop. B.17) give a mechanistic account of why agents can get trapped. The authors are commendably honest that the theorem formalizes the 'absence of a strong upward training signal' rather than monotone decrease (Remark B.15).

AREW is simple, well-derived, and cleanly connected to the theory: the margin-based auxiliary objective (Eq. 2) reduces to a per-step additive advantage reweighting (Eq. 5-6), so the method is implementable as a minimal modification to PPO/GRPO/GSPO. Proposition 4.1 nicely characterizes when the method helps via a 'weighted accuracy' of critiques, and this prediction is actually tested in the noise-perturbation experiments (Table 2).

The empirical evaluation is broad: 3 domains, 7 tasks, 3 RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), 2 model families (Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), with improvements in 27 of 28 settings, plus ablations on the reweighting strength and robustness to noisy critiques. Reproducibility is good: prompt templates, critique-construction rules, hyperparameters, and hardware details are all provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The BT critiques (and some AS critiques) rely on privileged ground-truth information at training time: the PE BT critique uses the ground-truth preference w*, and the MediQ/FloDial BT critiques use the ground-truth hypothesis s* (Appendix C.3). This makes AREW close to oracle-guided reward shaping and raises serious questions about applicability to tasks where step-level ground truth is unavailable — exactly the settings where outcome-only RL is most needed. The paper's framing of these as 'easy-to-obtain diagnostic signals' understates this dependence, and there is no experiment on a task lacking such signals.

The theory, while carefully done, rests on strong assumptions whose realism is not established: deterministic observation kernels (contradicting the LLM-simulated users actually used in experiments), query-independent self-destructive drift (Asmp. B.4), Lipschitz first-order expandability of the indices (Asmp. B.8), and bounded gradient norms. No empirical validation is offered for whether these hold, even approximately, in the testbeds, so the link between Thm. 3.4 and the observed dynamics remains qualitative.

Baseline coverage is thin on the most relevant competitors. The related-work section names CURIO, Sotopia-RL, and Spa-RL as approaches that also address intermediate/credit-assignment signals, yet none are compared. Simple exploration-strengthening alternatives (entropy bonuses, longer rollouts with GRPO variants partially cover this) or an oracle-critique upper bound are also missing, making it hard to judge how much of the gain is from the directional critiques specifically versus any extra dense signal.

Evaluation rigor has gaps: no error bars, standard deviations, or statement of the number of random seeds; several test sets appear very small (Table 1 reports multiples of ~1/30, suggesting ~30 test instances), so reported differences (e.g., MediQ 61.25 vs 57.25, FloDial-Easy 43.67 vs 41.00) may not be statistically meaningful. The MediQ and FloDial gains for Qwen are notably weaker than for PE tasks and for Llama.

Proposition 4.1's derivation drops cross-time terms 'for simplicity of analysis' (Appendix B.7), so the headline claim that improvement is 'fully determined' by weighted accuracy is approximate rather than exact; this should be stated as such in the main text. Additionally, the λu ablation shows training collapse at large values, indicating the method introduces a nontrivial hyperparameter sensitivity the paper defers to future work.

The core phenomenon, while well-named and well-illustrated, substantially overlaps with known pathologies in multi-turn RL (credit assignment masking, exploration collapse, interaction under-utilization as in Wang et al. 2025b and Hu et al. 2024). The novelty lies mainly in the AS/BT coupling framing and the specific reweighting mechanism, which is a moderate rather than fundamental contribution; the testbeds (synthetic preference estimation, LLM-simulated patients, small candidate sets) further limit evidence of generality to open-ended agentic settings.

strengths: The paper identifies and names a practically relevant failure mode (information self-locking) in outcome-based RL for multi-turn active reasoning, and the bidirectional AS/BT decomposition is a useful lens for diagnosis.

The empirical coverage is broad: 3 domains, 7 tasks, 2 model families, and 3 RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), with ablations on reweighting strength and critique-noise robustness that support the usefulness of the proposed technique.

The theory appendix is thorough and honest about being a one-sided, projected-drift characterization (Remark B.15), and Proposition 4.1/B.19 gives a clean characterization of when the auxiliary objective helps (weighted accuracy > 1/2).

The writing is generally clear, the method (advantage reweighting via a likelihood-margin auxiliary term) is simple, compatible with existing optimizers, and the prompt templates and critique constructions are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method's critiques are not purely environment-derived: the BT critique uses privileged ground-truth information (w*, s*, sim to the oracle preference) to assign directional labels, and the AS proxy in PE-G also compares against ground truth. This is effectively dense, ground-truth-informed reward shaping, which weakens the central 'outcome-only RL fails, our diagnostic signals fix it' narrative — the comparison against outcome-only baselines is not apples-to-apples, and this key caveat is not confronted directly.

The theoretical framework relies on strong, unverifiable assumptions (B.4–B.9: query-invariant self-destructive drift, bounded absorbed progress, Lipschitz stability, first-order expandability of indices that themselves involve oracle Bayesian beliefs). Theorem 3.4 is admitted to be informal, its quantities (I_th, C_BT) are not measurable in practice, and the result largely formalizes the intuition that weak signals stay weak; the escape-time corollary concerns 'projected evolutions consistent with the drift envelope' rather than actual training dynamics.

The empirical evidence for the headline claim is fragile: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, test sets appear very small (granularity of ~1–3 points, e.g., 24.00 vs 30.52), training runs are short (200 PPO steps), and 'up to 60%' improvements cherry-pick the largest relative gains from low baselines.

Missing baselines: the related-work section cites directly competing credit-assignment / shaping methods (SPA-RL, CURIO, Sotopia-RL, RLVRR) but none are compared empirically, so it is impossible to tell whether AREW's advantage reweighting is better than generic step-level shaping with the same privileged signals.

AS/BT proxies are heuristic and partly ground-truth-based, so proxy improvements (Fig. 4) could reflect proxy gaming or the injected signal rather than genuine capability growth; the confound is acknowledged only indirectly.

The experimental protocol heavily scaffolds the agent (alternating Action/Update rounds, instructed explicit confidence updates, prompted belief readout Ψ̂), which limits external validity to less structured agentic settings, and the paper offers no code release statement, hurting reproducibility of the multi-component setup.

Novelty is moderate: the failure mode overlaps with previously documented search/action degradation under outcome-only training (e.g., Wang et al. 2025b), and the remedy (per-step advantage reweighting from auxiliary labels) is a fairly standard credit-assignment mechanism applied to a new setting.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a novel and practically relevant failure mode ('information self-locking', SeL) in outcome-based RL for multi-turn active reasoning, decomposing agent behavior into action selection (AS) and belief tracking (BT) and showing bidirectional coupling that prevents either capability from improving — this diagnosis is a genuinely new contribution to understanding why outcome-only RL can fail in interactive settings.

The theoretical framework is substantive: the policy-gradient decomposition into AS/BT channels (Eq. 1), the 2D locking regime (Thm. 3.4 / B.14), the finite-escape-time lower bound (Prop. B.17), and the weighted-accuracy characterization of when AREW helps (Prop. B.19) are carefully developed, with assumptions stated explicitly and accompanied by intuitive discussion (Remarks B.15, B.16) and honest framing that the theorem bounds the magnitude of improvements rather than asserting strict trapping.

The proposed method (AREW) is elegant and minimal: a margin-aware auxiliary objective that reduces exactly to additive advantage reweighting (Eq. 5–6), requiring no extra rewards, discriminator models, or changes to the underlying RL optimizer; the centering property of the per-step coefficients is a nice technical detail.

Empirical evaluation is broad and largely convincing: 3 domains, 7 tasks, 2 model families (Qwen, Llama), 3 RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), ablations over reweighting strength λu, and a controlled noise-perturbation study (Table 2) that directly supports the weighted-accuracy theory; improvements are reported consistently (27 of 28 settings for AS+BT).

Reproducibility is strong: complete prompt templates (Figs. 6–8), dataset-specific critique construction rules, hyperparameters, hardware, and framework details are provided; the limitations around the λu trade-off are candidly discussed rather than hidden.

The interventional analyses (fixed action sequences with agent vs. oracle belief updates, replacing feedback with 'Unknown') provide credible causal evidence for the claimed coupling mechanism, going beyond correlational proxy plots.
weaknesses: The theory rests on idealized assumptions whose validity for LLM agents is debatable: deterministic feedback (O(s*, q)), Assumption B.4 (self-destructive drift invariant to query choice), Assumption B.5 (absorbed progress bounded by Cmax·C_BT), and Lipschitz/expansibility conditions. The result is a local, first-order upper-envelope bound on positive drift; it does not establish that vanilla RL remains locked (only that improvements within the regime are small), so the theoretical 'trapping' story is weaker than the narrative suggests.

The BT-side critiques rely on ground-truth quantities (w* in PE, s* in MediQ/FloDial) to label belief-update steps, and the AS critiques use hand-crafted, dataset-specific rules. While outcome rewards also require ground truth, this makes the method fundamentally tied to synthetic/verifiable environments with known answer spaces; the paper does not adequately discuss how critiques would be obtained in open-ended settings, which limits the claimed generality.

The benchmarks are small and stylized (finite attribute/hypothesis sets, ≤10 turns, rule-based simulated users, apparently small test sets judging by reward granularity), and some absolute gains are modest (e.g., FloDial-Easy 41.00→44.33 for Qwen); no comparison against existing process-reward or curiosity-based baselines (e.g., CURIO, Stopia-RL, SPA-RL, which are discussed in related work) is provided empirically, so it is hard to judge AREW's relative merit beyond vanilla outcome RL.

AS and BT measurement proxies are themselves human-defined heuristics (e.g., the AS 'informative comparison' indicator, 'Unknown'-feedback rules for FloDial), introducing potential circularity between the proxies used to diagnose SeL, the critiques used to fix it, and the metrics used to evaluate it.

Sensitivity analysis shows a narrow effective regime for λu: too small yields no escape from SeL and too large causes training collapse (Fig. 5d); the paper defers adaptive reweighting to future work, leaving a practical tuning burden.

The main text is notation-dense and the theoretical development (Definitions 3.1–3.2, channel-isolated advantages) is difficult to follow without the appendix, which may hinder accessibility; several important experimental details (e.g., number of test items, variance/significance of results in Table 1) are not clearly reported.

strengths: The paper identifies and carefully characterizes a genuinely interesting and practically relevant failure mode (information self-locking, SeL) in multi-turn active reasoning: reward improves while information acquisition (AS) and evidence internalization (BT) stagnate. The diagnostic experiments in Sec. 2.3, particularly the intervention where patient feedback is replaced with 'Unknown' to show reduced interaction-sensitivity after RL, and the strong-BT vs. agent-BT correlation analysis, are well designed and support the claimed bidirectional coupling.

The proposed method (AREW) is simple and well motivated: it derives stepwise coefficients from a likelihood-margin auxiliary objective and injects them as additive advantage shaping, preserving the outcome reward and critic target. The observation that the same weak directional signals are better used for credit reallocation than as direct intermediate rewards is empirically validated (Tables 3-4), which is a useful practical insight.

The experimental scope is broad: 4 domains / 9 tasks, two model families, three RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), a practical tau^2-bench evaluation with a dual-control setting that reveals a concrete instance of SeL (user-side repair shortcut), robustness analyses under random and structured critique perturbations, lambda sensitivity, belief-elicitation prompt variation, and a GPT-5 rubric-based re-evaluation to check that conclusions are not artifacts of hand-designed proxies.

The appendix treatment of related methods (connection to on-policy distillation, differences from reward shaping) is thoughtful and honest, and limitations such as the sensitivity to lambda are openly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The theory (Thm. 3.4 / C.15) leans on several strong, hard-to-verify assumptions (C.4-C.10), some of which essentially encode the desired conclusion. In particular, Assumption C.5 bounds absorbed progress by the current BT capability and Assumption C.6 bounds residual AS budget by global IAS, so the 'coupled bottleneck' inequality largely follows by construction. The escape-time result (Prop. C.18) is an upper-envelope argument that is quite loose. The theoretical contribution is more a formalization of intuition than a nontrivial prediction.

Proposition 4.1 / C.20 relies on a 'diagonal score-covariance approximation' that drops cross terms; the headline claim that AREW helps whenever weighted accuracy > 1/2 is therefore heuristic rather than rigorous, despite being presented as a characterization.

The critiques used in the main experiments are far less 'easy-to-obtain' than advertised: the BT critique on PE uses cosine similarity to the ground-truth preference w*, and on MediQ/FloDial the BT critique requires the ground-truth hypothesis s* (margin or counterfactual-vs-ground-truth checks). Per-step oracle access to ground truth in simulation does not transfer to realistic settings, weakening the practical significance of the headline gains; only the tau^2-bench instantiation uses benchmark-native signals.

Baseline coverage is thin relative to the related work the paper itself cites: process/stepwise reward methods such as SPA-RL, CURIO, RLVMR, and T3 (the latter closely related, from an overlapping group) are discussed but not empirically compared. The comparison to direct intermediate reward shaping appears only in the appendix on a subset of tasks.

Evidence quality concerns: no error bars, seeds, or statistical testing are reported; several test sets appear small given the granularity of reported jumps (e.g., 62-point gains on PE-G_S=3), and direct-inference baselines are very weak, suggesting possibly brittle task formatting. There are also presentation defects that undermine confidence: Fig. 8 plots 'Response Length' on the y-axis while the caption claims robustness in final performance, Fig. 9a's x-axis is mislabeled 'Rewards', the method name oscillates between AREW and AReW, and several citations carry implausible metadata (e.g., 'arXiv:2605.29782').

The lambda ablation shows AREW can collapse with overly aggressive reweighting, and the paper offers only a conjecture; a more principled treatment or adaptive scheme is deferred to future work, leaving a hyperparameter risk for practitioners.

strengths: The paper identifies and names a real and practically relevant failure mode (information self-locking) in outcome-based RL for interactive/active-reasoning LLM agents, and the empirical motivation (Sec. 2.3, Figs. 2 and 6a) — e.g., reduced sensitivity to intervened 'Unknown' feedback after RL, and higher AS-reward correlation under oracle belief updates — is thoughtfully designed and convincing.

The evaluation is broad: 9 tasks across 4 domains, two model families, three RL algorithms (PPO/GRPO/GSPO), plus robustness analyses (random sign flipping, structured perturbations in Fig. 8, critique-chasing scenarios in Tables 3–4) and a rubric-based cross-check of the AS/BT proxies using an external LLM (Table 5), which mitigates concerns about hand-crafted proxies.

The proposed injection mechanism is clean: the likelihood-margin auxiliary objective reduces exactly to an additive advantage shaping (A_t + λu_t), is reward-preserving, and the connection to on-policy distillation in Appendix A.1 gives useful context.
Reproducibility support is reasonable: code is released, prompts are provided in Appendix E, and training configurations are specified.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Thm. C.15) leans on assumptions that substantially pre-assume the conclusion. Assumption C.5 directly bounds one-step absorbed belief progress by the current BT capability, and Assumption C.4 postulates action-invariant harmful belief drift; together with C.6, these make Propositions C.11/C.12 almost immediate restatements. The 'self-locking' theorem is thus closer to a formalization of the assumptions than a nontrivial discovery, and the regularity assumptions (uniform first-order expandability on a parameter region, Lipschitz coupling) are not verified in practice.

The BT-side critique construction is arguably privileged supervision rather than an 'easy-to-obtain' weak signal: z_BT in Appendix E.3 is computed against ground-truth quantities (similarity to w*, margin on s*, counterfactual belief updates w_cf). This means the method injects dense, label-informed process supervision, which weakens the headline claim of a lightweight, calibration-free remedy and makes the comparison to genuine weak-signal settings less compelling.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the claims made. There are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests, while key numbers fluctuate substantially (e.g., Table 2: 80.3 → 40.0 → 65.0 across adjacent perturbation levels; PE-G_S=3 AREW jumps from 18.33 to 80.33). Several 'improvements' counted toward the 27/28 claim are marginal (LLaMA PE-F: 55.21 → 55.61, ↑0.4), and AREW–AS+BT underperforms AS-only on FloDial-Easy.

Missing baselines limit the significance assessment: related work cites direct competitors for intermediate/process credit (SPA-RL, CURIO, RLVMR, Wang et al. 2025b, T³, SOD) but none is compared empirically; the only dense-reward comparison is the authors' own intermediate-reward variant of the same critique. Without these, it is unclear whether AReW is preferable to existing credit-assignment methods.

The coherence of the paper across settings is uneven: the τ²-bench instantiation (Sec. 5.3) uses a completely different critique source (runtime tool failures, evaluator-exposed progress indicators) with no AS/BT proxy analysis, so it functions more as a loosely related application than as evidence for the SeL thesis; the reported 0.20 → 0.50 gain is not placed against published baselines.

Presentation issues: the method name alternates between AReW and AREW; the 'informal' main theorem defers everything to the appendix; and Fig. 2's claimed correlation differences are supported only by plots without quantitative correlation coefficients.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a genuinely relevant failure mode (information self-locking) for outcome-based RL in active reasoning, and the AS/BT decomposition is a clean, useful analytical lens that goes beyond anecdotal failure reports.

The empirical program is unusually thorough for this line of work: 7+ tasks across 4 domains, two model families (Qwen-2.5-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), three RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, GSPO), improvements in 27/28 settings, plus a practical extension to tau2-bench with both solo and dual-control settings.

Robustness analyses go well beyond the usual: random critique flipping, structured perturbations (channel/position/sign), comparison against direct intermediate reward injection on the same critique source, reward-hacking-style corruption tests, and sensitivity to the belief-elicitation prompt and reweighting strength lambda.

The theory is complemented by a practically useful characterization (Prop. 4.1/C.20): AREW works whenever critique weighted accuracy exceeds 1/2, which is directly validated by the noise-robustness experiments. The Appendix C proofs are complete and the mechanisms (BT-limited AS drift, AS-limited BT envelope) match the empirical observations.

The design choice of reward-preserving advantage reweighting (keeping critic and outcome reward untouched) is well motivated and empirically distinguished from intermediate reward shaping, including a plausible account of why it resists critique chasing.
Potential circularity in the hand-designed AS/BT proxies is addressed with an independent GPT-5 rubric-based evaluation (Table 5) showing the same qualitative trends.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: code availability is stated, hyperparameters, prompt templates, and critique construction rules are documented in detail (Appendix E).
weaknesses: The main theorem (Thm. 3.4/C.15) rests on a long list of assumptions (C.4-C.10), several of which are quite restrictive and not verifiable in practice (e.g., action-invariant harmful belief drift, residual AS-budget comparability with the global IAS). The result is essentially an upper bound on one-sided drifts, i.e., a statement about absence of strong signal, and the escape-time bound (Prop. C.18) is loose. The authors are somewhat honest about this in Remark C.16, but the gap between the formal result and the empirical phenomenon remains large.

The BT-side critiques and confidence readout implicitly rely on ground-truth s* during training (e.g., 'the confidence assigned to the ground-truth candidate s* induces Psi_bt when training labels provide s*'), and some MediQ critiques require counterfactual rollouts. This is a material assumption for the method's applicability to settings without labeled ground truth, and deserves a more explicit limitations discussion; the claim of 'easy-to-obtain' critiques holds cleanly mainly for the AS channel.

No error bars, seed counts, or significance tests are reported for the RL training results, which are known to be high-variance; several gains (e.g., some AS-ONLY results in Table 1, and the small, non-monotonic differences in Table 2) could be within noise.

The abstract claims '9 agentic tasks' while the main table reports 7; minor but should be reconciled. Similarly, 'up to 60-point gains' is driven by tasks where the vanilla baseline is near-zero, which inflates the headline number.

There is no empirical comparison against existing process-reward / stepwise-credit methods (SPA-RL, CURIO, Sotopia-RL, RLVMR) beyond a conceptual discussion and a self-constructed intermediate-reward baseline, so the relative position of AREW within the credit-assignment literature is not established experimentally.

The practical generality of the method depends on task-specific critique design; the paper demonstrates this for its domains and tau2-bench, but the transferability of critique construction to open-ended environments remains untested.
